title: From Turbo C++ to Modern Web: Why Writing a DOS GUI in 2016 Shaped My Career as an Engineer
subtitle: How low-level pixel math, 16-bit memory limits, and graphics.h taught me more about UI architecture, rendering engines, and state machines than any modern JavaScript framework.
content:
Back in 2016, when the modern web was already in the midst of a component-driven revolution—with React 15 conquering the world, Webpack bundling everything in sight, and CSS-in-JS emerging—I decided to take a deliberate, nostalgic detour backwards: I spent months building a complete graphical windowing system from scratch in Turbo C++ 3.0 running under MS-DOS.

"To truly master modern abstractions, you must understand the hardware constraints that forced those abstractions to be invented in the first place."

1. The Constraint of Absolute Zero Frameworks

In modern web development, creating a button with a drop shadow, hover transition, and centered text is three lines of Tailwind CSS: className="shadow-lg hover:scale-105 flex items-center justify-center". The browser's layout engine handles subpixel rendering, antialiasing, layout reflows, compositing layers, and GPU acceleration transparently.

In Turbo C++ running in 16-bit real mode under DOS, you are handed nothing more than an unaccelerated 640x480 VGA video buffer (mode VGAHI) and Borland's primitive graphics.h header.

If you want a button with a drop shadow, there is no CSS shadow blur. You must:

  1. Calculate the exact Cartesian bounding box: (x1, y1, x2, y2).
  2. Fill a solid rectangle at (x1 + offset, y1 + offset, x2 + offset, y2 + offset) with color DARKGRAY to emulate the shadow.
  3. Fill the main button rectangle with LIGHTGRAY.
  4. Draw white lines along the top and left edges to represent light source specular highlights, and black lines along the bottom and right edges to represent bevel shading.
  5. Calculate the exact pixel width of the label string and position text using outtextxy(x + (w - textwidth(str))/2, y + (h - textheight(str))/2, str).

2. Deconstructing the Rendering Pipeline

Here is an exact excerpt from the DOS.CPP codebase showing how 3D-beveled window containers were rendered mathematically:

// Low-level window drawing routine in Turbo C++
void drawWindow(int x, int y, int w, int h, char* title) {
    // 1. Drop shadow offset
    setfillstyle(SOLID_FILL, DARKGRAY);
    bar(x + 5, y + 5, x + w + 5, y + h + 5);
    
    // 2. Main Window Surface
    setfillstyle(SOLID_FILL, LIGHTGRAY);
    bar(x, y, x + w, y + h);
    
    // 3. Beveled 3D Borders (Classic Windows 95 Aesthetic)
    setcolor(WHITE);
    line(x, y, x + w, y); // Top highlight line
    line(x, y, x, y + h); // Left highlight line
    setcolor(BLACK);
    line(x + w, y, x + w, y + h); // Right shadow line
    line(x, y + h, x + w, y + h); // Bottom shadow line
    
    // 4. Gradient Title Bar
    setfillstyle(SOLID_FILL, BLUE);
    bar(x + 2, y + 2, x + w - 2, y + 22);
    setcolor(WHITE);
    outtextxy(x + 10, y + 7, title);
}

3. The Pain of Dirty Rectangles and Frame Invalidation

One of the most profound lessons came from implementing window dragging and modal dialogs. When a user opened a dropdown menu or dragged a window across the screen, it obliterated the pixels underneath. Because there was no automatic DOM tree or layer compositing:

  • You had to allocate a chunk of precious 16-bit heap memory using imagesize(x, y, x2, y2) and malloc().
  • Call getimage(x, y, x2, y2, buffer) to snapshot the underlying canvas before drawing the popup.
  • When the popup closed, call putimage(x, y, buffer, COPY_PUT) to restore the background, followed by free(buffer) to prevent fatal memory leaks.

4. Architectural Takeaways for Modern Web Engineering

Working through those low-level constraints irrevocably shaped how I write code today across React, Vue, TypeScript, and native Swift:

A. Empathy for Browser Paint & Composite Cycles

When you have manually managed dirty rectangles and watched screen flicker when redraw loops miss raster synchronization, you understand why CSS transform and opacity are hardware-accelerated on GPU composite layers, while mutating width, height, or top triggers expensive CPU layout reflows.

B. UI as a Pure State Machine

In Turbo C++, if an event handler misses a state transition, the entire screen becomes an unrecoverable corrupted mess of pixels. This instilled in me a deep discipline for predictable state architectures: whether using Zustand in React, Vuex/Pinia in Vue, or Combine in Swift, UI must always be treated as a pure, deterministic projection of state over time.

C. Appreciation for WebGL & Canvas Primitives

When I later built complex WebGL 3D scenes (like the Hyper Mode on this portfolio) and custom Cytoscape graph parsing engines, the coordinate transformations and vertex math felt like second nature because the foundation had been forged in raw C++ geometry years prior.

5. Conclusion

Never hesitate to explore old or constrained technologies. Building under severe limitations strips away the illusion of magic in modern frameworks, leaving you with a durable, foundational mental model of how computers actually put pixels on glass.

title: Building SleepX: How We Engineered a Smart Travel Pillow & Reached Global Maker Finals
subtitle: From breadboard prototypes and 72-hour battery optimization to industrial rexine fabrication, pitching at Maker Mela, and competing in Shenzhen.
content:
Humans are social beings. And so, they travel from place to place for various purposes. During our undergraduate years at Toc H Institute of Science & Technology, my co-founder Siddharth Prajosh C and I spent hundreds of hours traveling on overnight intercity buses and trains across South India. The journey experience was universally plagued by friction: tangled earphone wires catching on luggage, phone batteries dying halfway through the night, and the inability to read books after overhead lights were extinguished.

We asked ourselves a simple question: What if the neck pillow you rest your head on became the hub for your entire journey experience?

🏆 Top 30 Finalist at Maker Mela 2018 (Mumbai)

⭐ Top 15 Finalist at Nanshan Entrepreneurship Star Contest (Shenzhen, China)

1. The 4 Engineering Pillars of SleepX

✨ Look Elegant & Water-Resistant

Handcrafted from fine rexine for comfort and filled with smooth polyester fiber. The rexine enables easy water cleaning and protects internal electronics from sweat or rain.

🔋 Run All Day Long (72+ Hours)

Powered by a 2,750mAh Li-ion battery, SleepX runs for over 3 days on a single charge. Charges via standard Micro-USB with ordinary smartphone chargers or power banks.

🎧 Let's Go Wireless (Bluetooth 4.0)

Inbuilt Bluetooth earphones with tactile side micro-switches to adjust volume, skip music tracks, and attend incoming phone calls hands-free.

💡 Optical Night Reading Lamp

Equipped with a focused white LED in a precision 45-degree engineered holder that illuminates books on your lap without spilling light onto adjacent passengers.

2. Hands-Free Voice Control

Control everything by voice! Users can summon Google Assistant on Android or Siri on iOS via the microphone and headset controls, eliminating the need to take phones out of pockets during crowded journeys.

3. The Maker Team Behind SleepX

"We are young makers from God's own Country — Kerala. We love making gadgets that seem fun and help us in our daily life. In our free time, we spend time taking classes and organising workshops for students on using technology to improve life."

Yadev Jayachandran

Hardware & Electronics

Siddharth Prajosh C

Embedded Systems

4. Key Lessons for Hardware Creators

  1. Solve Real Human Friction: SleepX wasn't built for the sake of IoT buzzwords; it was born out of 10-hour bumpy bus rides where our own ears hurt and batteries died.
  2. Ergonomics Beats Raw Specs: If a wearable device is uncomfortable for 10 minutes, users will discard it regardless of how advanced the circuitry is.
  3. Iterate in the Physical World: Building physical hardware teaches patience, precision, and respect for mechanical and thermal constraints.

title: Crafting Zero-Latency Native macOS Utilities: Inside macbar and FloatMe
subtitle: How to harness SwiftUI, AppKit window levels, and AVFoundation to build buttery-smooth Mac system tools with near-zero CPU overhead.
content:
When building desktop tools like macbar (turning your MacBook's camera notch into an expandable Dynamic Island HUD) and FloatMe (a zero-latency floating presenter camera), web-wrapper frameworks like Electron or webviews simply fall short. To build utilities that feel like they were shipped by Apple's core OS engineering team, you must dive deep into pure SwiftUI, AppKit, and Darwin system APIs.

🚀 Key Rule: A system utility should consume less than 1% CPU on idle, take under 25MB RAM, and never drop a single frame during display transitions.

1. Overcoming macOS Window Level Constraints

In macOS, full-screen applications like Keynote, PowerPoint, or full-screen IDE windows generate isolated virtual desktop spaces. Standard NSWindow instances are immediately concealed when the user switches spaces.

To build FloatMe so that your presenter video circle floats persistently over even full-screen slide presentations, we elevate the window level directly to the system screensaver tier:

// Configuring a persistent, space-agnostic floating window in Swift
let window = NSWindow(
    contentRect: NSRect(x: 100, y: 100, width: circleSize, height: circleSize),
    styleMask: [.borderless],
    backing: .buffered,
    defer: false
)

// Pinning to screenSaver layer guarantees visibility above full-screen apps
window.level = .screenSaver
window.collectionBehavior = [
    .canJoinAllSpaces,
    .fullScreenAuxiliary,
    .stationary,
    .ignoresCycle
]
window.isOpaque = false
window.backgroundColor = .clear

2. Implementing 'Ghost Mode': Click-Through Event Passing

One of the biggest frustrations with floating camera overlays is that they block interactive buttons underneath (such as a 'Run Test' button in Xcode or a slide navigation arrow in Keynote). FloatMe solves this with a seamless Ghost Mode toggle:

// Dynamically toggle event passing without disrupting video rendering
window.ignoresMouseEvents = isGhostModeActive

When ignoresMouseEvents is true, the window server allows cursor clicks and scroll events to pass directly through the circular video stream and hit whatever application element lies directly below.

3. Geometry Math for the MacBook Camera Notch

For macbar, aligning an expandable HUD flush with the physical MacBook notch requires calculating hardware screen cutouts at runtime. Rather than hardcoding pixel offsets, macbar queries NSScreen auxiliary areas:

  • screen.auxiliaryTopLeftArea: Extracts the exact left ear frame where media track titles and status icons are docked.
  • screen.auxiliaryTopRightArea: Extracts the right ear frame for battery health, Wi-Fi SSID, and clock displays.
  • Velocity-Sensitive Hover Tracking: Uses custom CoreGraphics event taps to check mouse deceleration before animating the expanded card, preventing accidental triggers during normal cursor navigation.

4. Real-Time Hardware Telemetry Without Shell Spawning

Many system monitors spawn background shell commands like top -l 1 or vm_stat every second, causing continuous CPU spikes and waking up power cores. macbar communicates directly with the Mach kernel:

// Direct Mach kernel CPU load polling in Swift
var cpuInfo = host_cpu_load_info()
var count = mach_msg_type_number_t(MemoryLayout<host_cpu_load_info_data_t>.size / MemoryLayout<integer_t>.size)
let kerr = withUnsafeMutablePointer(to: &cpuInfo) {
    $0.withMemoryRebound(to: integer_t.self, capacity: Int(count)) {
        host_statistics(mach_host_self(), HOST_CPU_LOAD_INFO, $0, &count)
    }
}

5. Summary

Building high-performance native macOS software requires respecting the operating system's native paradigms. By leveraging AppKit window servers, Metal shaders, and Mach kernel APIs, you can build delightful utilities that run invisibly and effortlessly in the background.

title: The Community Multiplier: Mentoring 500+ Developers Across Kerala with KSUM & Mozilla
subtitle: What organizing Idea Fest, Think Camp design bootcamps, and decentralized campus nodes taught me about developer ecosystems and leadership.
content:
During my tenure as a Technology Innovation Fellow at the Kerala Startup Mission (KSUM) and as Head of Design & Co-organizer of Mozilla Kerala, my core mission was simple yet ambitious: bridge the chasm between academic theory and real-world product building for student developers across the state.

"Great engineers are rarely forged by memorizing textbooks; they are created when peer learning meets authentic user problems."

1. The Campus 'Node' Model

Traditional college workshops often fail because they are one-off weekend lectures that leave no lasting habit. At Toc H and across 10+ campuses during Inspire 2019, we introduced a decentralized, peer-led learning model called Nodes:

  • Daily Lunch-Break Sprints: Instead of exhausting 8-hour sessions, students met for 30 minutes every day during lunch breaks to work on concrete coding and design challenges.
  • Hacktoberfest Onboarding: We introduced version control fundamentals (Git & GitHub) and mentored 28+ first-time open-source contributors in their first month alone.
  • Pay-It-Forward Mentorship: Senior students who mastered cloud fundamentals (GCP/AWS) or Machine Learning (via Google MLCC) were tasked with training the next incoming cohort, creating a self-sustaining cycle of peer education.

2. Scaling Idea Fest 2019: 1,800+ Teams & 30+ Funded Startups

As part of the KSUM fellowship, I co-organized Idea Fest 2019, the flagship student entrepreneurship platform for Kerala. The scale was exhilarating:

  • 1,800+ applied student teams submitting technology and product concepts from across all districts.
  • 150+ shortlisted finalist teams pitching to panels of venture capitalists, government officials, and technical architects.
  • 30+ student ventures funded with direct government innovation grants to build their working prototypes.

3. Design Thinking & Think Camp

In partnership with Design4India and Lumium Design, we conducted Think Camp, an immersive 1-day design thinking bootcamp series. We taught engineering students how to stop writing code prematurely and instead focus on user empathy, journey mapping, and rapid paper prototyping.

To support this, I created and open-sourced ProDeck—a structured set of ideation frameworks that guided students through problem deconstruction, perspective shifting, and feasibility scoring.

4. What Community Leadership Taught Me as an Engineer

Serving as Co-organizer & Head of Design for Mozilla Kerala, leading developer communities, organizing hackathons (such as WhyHack for women in technology), and designing open-source brand identities fundamentally altered how I operate as a senior software engineer today:

  1. Clarity of Communication: If you can explain complex distributed systems or machine learning concepts to a first-year student, you can write world-class technical RFCs and documentation for your engineering team.
  2. Empathy-Driven Engineering: Watching hundreds of novice users struggle with poorly designed tools reinforces why user experience and intuitive interface design are non-negotiable.
  3. Culture is Everything: An engineering team with psychological safety and strong peer-mentorship culture will out-ship a team of isolated geniuses every single time.
